project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first recognition module with seven project-pool genus doors
project_scope.note: The family lesson uses flower/ovary/fruit architecture, then splits into Solanum, Physalis, Datura, Nicotiana, Chamaesaracha, Capsicum and Bouchetia patterns. Native/introduced status remains a separate species-level question.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Look for a fused usually 5-lobed corolla with usually 5 stamens attached to the corolla, then confirm a superior usually 2-carpellate ovary with many ovules. Fruit is usually a many-seeded berry or capsule and the calyx often persists or enlarges.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Herbs, shrubs, small trees or climbers; leaves usually alternate, simple to lobed or divided, and without stipules. Hairs may be simple, glandular, branched or stellate; prickles occur in some Solanum.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers mostly bisexual and 5-merous. Corolla lobes are fused; stamens alternate with the lobes. Anthers open by longitudinal slits or apical pores depending on genus.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Usually a many-seeded berry or capsule. Persistent/accrescent calyces are common and become extreme in Physalis.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Family first: fused 5-part flower + superior many-ovuled ovary + berry/capsule. Genus second: poricidal anthers, inflated calyx, giant trumpet, tobacco tube, or five-eyes habit.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: fused flower → anthers/ovary → fruit type → genus doors → Convolvulaceae/Boraginaceae comparisons
visual_lesson.intro: Nightshades become much easier when you stop identifying them by flower color and instead read the anthers, calyx and fruit.

steps.title: 1 · Solanum door: look straight at the anther cone
steps.image_label: Solanum poricidal anthers around the style
steps.look_for: Five anthers gathered around the style, each opening near the tip by pores rather than long side slits.
steps.why_it_matters: Poricidal anthers are a powerful Solanum clue and connect directly to buzz pollination.

steps.title: 2 · Physalis door: follow the calyx into fruit
steps.look_for: The calyx enlarges dramatically after flowering and becomes a bladder-like husk that completely encloses the berry.
steps.why_it_matters: An inflated fruiting calyx is the fastest project-pool route to Physalis.

steps.title: 3 · Datura door: giant funnel flower → prickly capsule
steps.look_for: Very large white funnel/trumpet flowers followed by a dry capsule, commonly armed with prickles.
steps.why_it_matters: Datura is a capsule-producing nightshade and looks nothing like berry-producing Solanum or Physalis once fruiting.

steps.title: 4 · Nicotiana door: long tube → capsule
steps.photo_role: tubular corolla + persistent calyx around capsule
steps.look_for: Tubular to funnelform flowers, often on viscid/hairy plants, followed by a dry capsule mostly enclosed by the persistent calyx.
steps.why_it_matters: This separates tobacco architecture from the starry berry-producing nightshades.

steps.title: 5 · Chamaesaracha door: low five-eyes
steps.photo_role: prostrate habit + pale rotate corolla + exposed berry
steps.look_for: Low spreading plants with pale rotate flowers; the calyx enlarges somewhat in fruit but does not inflate into a Physalis lantern and remains shorter than the berry.
steps.why_it_matters: It is an excellent local comparison for Physalis and Solanum.

comparisons.title: Solanaceae vs Convolvulaceae
comparisons.rule: Both often have fused funnel-shaped corollas. Solanaceae typically has a superior usually 2-locular ovary with many ovules and a berry/capsule; morning-glory relatives often twine and have different ovary/fruit architecture.

comparisons.title: Solanaceae vs Boraginaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have fused 5-part flowers. Classic Boraginaceae often has a scorpioid cyme and four nutlets; Solanaceae usually makes a many-seeded berry or capsule. Broad Boraginaceae includes capsular exceptions, so use the whole reproductive pattern.

comparisons.title: Solanum vs Physalis
comparisons.rule: Solanum usually advertises a starry corolla and poricidal anther cone with the berry exposed; Physalis completely encloses the berry in a greatly inflated papery calyx.

comparisons.title: Physalis vs Chamaesaracha
comparisons.rule: Physalis fruiting calyx becomes bladder-like and fully encloses the berry; Chamaesaracha has an accrescent but non-inflated calyx that remains shorter than the berry.

visual_lesson.caveat: Solanaceae is chemically and morphologically diverse; flower color, prickles, toxicity, or edible fruit are not family-level identification characters. Use reproductive structure.
